contentMarkdown:
A text to PDF converter online free turns plain words into a proper document in under a minute — no word processor to open, no account to create, and no file to upload. You type or paste your text, style it with headings and lists, set the page size, and download a clean PDF that looks like you designed it. This guide walks through the fastest free method, the formatting options that make the result look professional, and the honest limits to know before you start.

![Writing with a fountain pen on paper before turning the text into a PDF](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1455390582262-044cdead277a?w=1200&q=80)

## How to convert text to PDF free in 3 steps

The whole job happens in your browser, so your text never leaves your device.

### Step 1: Open the converter and add your text

Open the [free Text to PDF converter](/tools/text-to-pdf) and type straight into the editor, or paste text from anywhere — notes app, email, chat, a document. If you already have the words in a file, use **Import TXT** to load a `.txt` or `.md` file instead of typing. Short on time? Start from a template — **Formal letter**, **Meeting notes**, or **Simple report** — and replace the sample text with your own.

### Step 2: Style each block

Click any block to select it, then use the formatting toolbar: **H1, H2, or H3** for headings, **B** and **I** for bold and italic, left, center, or justify alignment, and font sizes from 10 to 18 pt. Bullet and numbered lists, quotes, checklists, dividers, and page breaks are all one click away. Press Enter inside a paragraph to split it into two blocks; empty a block and hit Backspace to remove it. A live preview on the side shows exactly what the downloaded PDF will look like, so there are no layout surprises.

### Step 3: Set the filename and download

Give the document a filename, glance at the live preview, and press **Download PDF**. Pagination is automatic, so a long document flows across pages on its own. The file downloads straight to your device — no sign-up, no watermark, and no page limit.

## Make the PDF look professional: formatting that matters

A plain dump of text reads like a draft. Four settings turn it into a document you can send to someone.

### Headings and structure

Break the text into headed sections. A cover letter gets an H1 title and H2 sections; meeting notes get an H2 per agenda item with bullet lists for the action points underneath. Bold the key terms in study notes so they stand out when you skim. Structure is what separates a readable PDF from a wall of text.

### Page setup: size, margins, and fonts

Open **Advanced PDF settings** and pick a page size — A4, Letter, Legal, or A5 — in portrait or landscape. Margins come in narrow, normal, and wide presets, or set your own. Three fonts are available: Helvetica for a clean modern look, Times for formal documents, and Courier for a typewriter feel. You can also adjust line spacing, paragraph spacing, and first-line indent, plus page background and text colours.

### Headers, footers, and page numbers

Add header and footer text — a document title, your name, a date — and page numbers in one of three formats: a plain number, "Page 1 of 3", or "– 1 –". On a multi-page document this is the detail that makes it look finished rather than thrown together.

### Watermarks and stamps

The output carries no watermark unless you add one yourself. If you want one — "DRAFT", "CONFIDENTIAL", a company name — the advanced settings let you add it deliberately, rather than having a converter stamp its own logo on your work.

## Text to PDF on iPhone and Android

The converter runs entirely in your mobile browser, so there is no app to install. On iPhone, open it in Safari, type or paste your text, and download the PDF — it lands in the Files app under Downloads. On Android, the same steps work in Chrome, with the file saved to your Downloads folder. The editor and the live preview both work on a phone screen, though a long document is easier to style on a bigger display.

## Import a TXT or Markdown file instead of typing

If your text already lives in a `.txt` or `.md` file, import it and skip the typing entirely. The content arrives as editable blocks you can restyle before downloading — the quickest route for meeting logs, scripts, and notes you already keep as plain text.

## When text to PDF beats opening a word processor

A word processor is the right tool for a 40-page report. For everything smaller, the browser converter is faster:

- **Cover letters and resumes** — paste your draft, turn section titles into headings, export a clean PDF to attach to a job application.
- **Homework and study notes** — paste revision notes, split topics into headed blocks, bold the key terms, and print a PDF that is far easier to read than plain text.
- **Minutes of meetings** — turn a running log into a shareable PDF in one click, with headings for agenda items and bullet lists for action points.
- **Scripts and manuscripts** — writers and video creators convert drafts to PDF for editors and collaborators; justified alignment and real headings give it a typeset feel.
- **Quick receipts and notices** — type a packing list, a simple receipt, or a printable notice as bullet blocks, download, and print. Faster than launching a word processor for two paragraphs.

## Text to PDF vs Word to PDF: pick the right tool

These two sound alike and solve different problems. Use the text converter when your starting point is plain text you type or paste. If you already have a `.docx` file, convert that file directly with the [free Word to PDF converter](/tools/word-to-pdf-converter) instead — retyping it into the text editor would waste the formatting Word already has. And if your text is trapped in a photo or a scan, run it through the [image to text tool](/tools/image-to-text) first, then paste the result here.

## The honest limits

Three things to know. First, this is a text editor that makes clean, simply formatted documents — not a full word processor, so a complex layout with tables and embedded images belongs in Word or Google Docs, then converted with Word to PDF. Second, pasting from a word processor brings the words across as text; reapply headings and bold with the toolbar rather than expecting the original formatting to survive. Third, the converter only handles text you can type, paste, or import as `.txt`/`.md` — it cannot open a `.docx`, a scanned image, or a PDF. Pick the matching tool for those, and the text converter does exactly what it promises, with nothing uploaded and nothing watermarked.

## Try it now

If you have text that needs to become a PDF, the quickest test takes about a minute: open the [free Text to PDF converter](/tools/text-to-pdf), paste a paragraph, make one line a heading, and download it. If the result looks the way you wanted, you have your workflow — no install, no account, and the file never leaves your browser.
